analysis.one_liner: Makes giant gig companies withhold and pay Social Security and Medicare taxes on contractor pay.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote or a floor vote and died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: Companies with at least $100 million in annual revenue and at least 10,000 independent contractors would have to treat contractor pay like wages for payroll taxes. The company would pay the employer share of Social Security and Medicare taxes (12.4% and 2.9% combined under the bill's rates) and withhold the worker's share from payments. Gig workers at very large platforms would build Social Security and Medicare coverage on that income, which they currently must pay for entirely out of their own pocket as self-employment tax. The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Independent contractors working for very large gig companies, such as ride-hailing and delivery platforms. Their pay would be reported and taxed as wages: the company pays the employer half of Social Security and Medicare taxes, and the worker's half is withheld from pay. Contractors would still count these earnings toward Social Security and Medicare the way employees do, without having to set aside money for the employer share themselves.

how_it_helps.text: Applies to companies with $100 million or more in gross receipts and at least 10,000 independent contractors, treating payments to those contractors as wages for payroll tax purposes [S3].
The company would owe the employer share of Social Security and Medicare taxes, and the worker's share would be withheld, so contractors no longer bear the full self-employment tax alone [S3].
Earnings treated as wages under the bill are counted toward Social Security benefits, giving contractors the same coverage as regular employees for those earnings [S3].
The rules apply to companies under common ownership as a single employer, closing a route around the threshold [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Very large gig platforms and other big companies that rely on contractor labor, which would owe the employer share of payroll taxes on contractor payments and handle wage-style withholding. Some of that cost could show up as lower rates, fees, or fewer contract opportunities for workers.

drawbacks.text: Withholding the employee share would immediately reduce contractors' take-home pay, a real squeeze for workers living paycheck to paycheck, even though the money builds future Social Security and Medicare coverage [S3].

The bill taxes workers like employees for payroll purposes without giving them the employment protections that come with employee status, such as minimum wage, overtime, or unemployment insurance [S3].
The employer share is a new cost per payment for affected companies, which could be passed on through higher prices or reduced contractor opportunities [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real: gig workers at the largest platforms would stop carrying the entire payroll tax burden alone and would build Social Security and Medicare credits like employees do. The main costs fall on the companies, though part can be passed back to workers through take-home pay and prices, and the bill leaves gig workers without employee protections even as it taxes them like employees. A targeted fix for a real gap, not a comprehensive one.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced on October 22, 2021 by Rep. Bonnie Watson Coleman with 9 Democratic cosponsors [S1] [S4].
Referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day; that was the bill's last action [S5].
No markup, vote, or floor action followed before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large gig platforms and contractor-heavy companies keep paying no employer share of payroll taxes on contractor pay. Gig workers keep paying the full self-employment tax out of their own pockets.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Big gig platforms that avoid payroll taxes

for.name: Rep. Bonnie Watson Coleman
for.role: Sponsor, House Ways and Means Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill requiring large companies to withhold and pay payroll taxes on contractor pay.

against.name: Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of referral under Chairman Richard Neal (D)
against.what_they_did: Never held a markup or vote on the bill; it sat in committee until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 9 cosponsors were Democrats, and no Republican support is recorded; the bill was a one-party effort that never advanced [S4].

industries.note: The bill would make the largest platforms pay the employer share of Social Security and Medicare taxes on contractor payments and run wage-style withholding, a direct cost on their contractor-based business model. Workers gain coverage, which is why the industry's interest runs against the public's here.
Large-scale wage-style withholding for hundreds of thousands of contractors would require payroll systems and compliance services.
